However, there are similarities between the concept of brute forcing a password and genetically modifying things through sequential iterations of modifications of a DNA base pair. Of course, you can cut out the waste of trying the 'synonyms' by knowing what protein it will make. Monsanto does something along the lines of 'brute force' in their corn research. When they try to genetically modify corn, they modify a batch, some lab grunt grows it, and notes any changes in things they find useful. Health of the plant, water retention, etc. It's not very fast, a computer might be able to set up a list of all the changes they'd like to try out and go through in millions of combinations, but someone still has to grow it to see what it does.

It's safe to assume that any modern technique is being tried across the board, to solve problems in all domains.

What makes cracking an encrypted message easier than deciphering an ancient language? With a modern language, you can assume that the result is a plaintext in some modern language. Any modern language has well-known statistical distributions of letters, words, and word order, so knowing this makes a huge difference in terms of speeding up a program-backed brute force search. For one, if you're trying out input combinations, you know which ones to try first, and if you're checking output patterns, your program can automatically see which ones are far more likely to be valid than others.

You don't have the same thing to work with when you're working with an ancient language. At best, you have similar languages to compare to. Otherwise, you're stuck trying to decipher at the concept level rather than at the word level, and that's far more complex to encode, and thus far more difficult for a program to recognize.
